items.title: About 90% of your serotonin is made in your gut
items.claim: Serotonin is famous as a mood-related brain chemical. But ~90% of the body's serotonin is in the gut, where it regulates gut motility and is influenced by gut bacteria. The gut and brain communicate via the vagus nerve and circulating molecules.

options.text: A direct neural connection like an optic nerve

A multi-channel system: vagus nerve sends ~80% afferent (gut-to-brain) signals; immune signalling; circulating short-chain fatty acids and neurotransmitters from gut bacteria — all influence brain function bidirectionally
A myth — the gut and brain don't talk

items.reveal_title: The enteric nervous system and microbial signals
items.reveal:
The gut has its own nervous system (the enteric nervous system, ENS) with ~500 million neurons — about as many as a cat's brain. The ENS controls gut motility, secretion and absorption largely independently of the central nervous system.

The vagus nerve connects gut and brain. About 80% of vagus fibres are afferent (carrying signals FROM gut TO brain). Gut chemical and stretch receptors continuously inform the brain about digestive state.

Serotonin: ~90% is in enterochromaffin cells of the gut, regulating peristalsis and pain signalling. Drugs targeting gut serotonin (e.g., 5-HT3 antagonists) treat IBS and chemotherapy nausea.

Gut bacteria contribute by:
- Producing short-chain fatty acids (butyrate, propionate) from fibre, which affect blood-brain barrier permeability and microglial function.
- Producing or modulating neurotransmitters (GABA, serotonin precursors).
- Influencing tryptophan metabolism (the precursor for serotonin).
- Modulating systemic inflammation.

Germ-free mice (raised without bacteria) show altered behaviour, anxiety, and brain development — restored by giving them normal gut bacteria. Effects in humans are more modest but real (e.g., faecal microbiota transplants can influence mood markers in some patients).

The gut-brain field is young and much remains speculative. Causal direction and effect sizes in humans are still being mapped.
items.why: Brain chemistry feels like brain-only territory. Much of our serotonin is in the gut; bacteria influence brain function via multiple routes. The body's signalling architecture is broader than its anatomy suggests.

items.title: Bacteria swap genes like trading cards
items.claim: Sexual reproduction is supposedly biology's great innovation for mixing genes. Bacteria don't bother. They share DNA fragments — including whole antibiotic-resistance genes — directly between unrelated species, sometimes across genera.

options.text: Useful mutations spread across the bacterial 'pan-genome' far faster than vertical inheritance allows — antibiotic resistance can jump from one species to another in a single transfer event
Bacteria only share genes within the same species
Horizontal transfer is too rare to matter

items.reveal_title: Three mechanisms keep the bacterial gene pool fluid
items.reveal:
Conjugation: two bacteria form a physical bridge (pilus) and transfer a plasmid.
Transformation: bacteria scoop up loose DNA from the environment.
Transduction: viruses (phages) accidentally package bacterial DNA and inject it into the next host.

The NDM-1 resistance gene, first found in Klebsiella in 2008, jumped via plasmids across at least 11 bacterial species and 4 continents within a decade. Genes encoding beta-lactamases (penicillin breakdown) appear in soil bacteria; clinical pathogens picked them up after antibiotics entered hospitals.

The 'tree of life' for bacteria isn't really a tree — it's a tangled net.
items.why: Evolution is taught as descent with modification along branching lineages. Bacterial evolution is reticular — sideways, not just downward.

items.title: Your liver and your eyes have separate clocks
items.claim: Every cell in your body has its own molecular clock. The 'master' clock in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) synchronises them. Eating at the wrong time can desynchronise organs from each other — same as jet lag without the travel.
items.prompt: What is a cellular circadian clock made of?

options.text: A transcription-translation feedback loop: genes (BMAL1/CLOCK in mammals) drive expression of inhibitor proteins (PER, CRY) that themselves repress the original genes — the cycle takes about 24 hours to complete
An internal sundial of pigment molecules

items.reveal:
In Drosophila, Hall, Rosbash and Young identified Period (PER) gene and worked out the negative feedback loop: PER protein accumulates in the cell, eventually shuts down its own transcription, then degrades, allowing the cycle to repeat. Mammals have BMAL1/CLOCK driving PER1/2/3 and CRY1/2, with the same logic.

The cycle's intrinsic period is close to 24 hours; light input (via melanopsin in retinal ganglion cells) synchronises it to the day.

Peripheral clocks (in liver, muscle, fat) entrain primarily to feeding times. Eating at midnight tells your liver it's daytime even as your SCN says it's night — exactly the desynchronisation seen in shift workers, who have elevated rates of metabolic disease and some cancers.
items.why: The biological clock is pictured as one master organ. Every cell has one, and keeping them aligned is a daily ongoing process — and easily disrupted.
